         2. Ms Stein's affidavit describes her inspections of the property and her observations regarding the fresh disturbance of soil due to construction, the absence of adequate sediment and erosion controls including failing batters and lack of compaction of soil. She describes new roads being cut and sediment being placed into natural watercourse crossings, sediment deposits being placed in dry watercourses, and sediment dispersing downslope into gullies and dry watercourses. It exhibits a map showing the locations of her observations, and reproduces a "Notice of preventative action" issued to the defendants on 7 December 2017 pursuant to s 96 of the POEO Act, which indicated that Water NSW reasonably suspected that Kiangatha's construction of a road network was "causing sediment to be in a position where it has washed or is likely to be washed into tributaries of the Coxs River…".
         3. Mr Draper's affidavit describes the identification of Kiangatha's property, his inspections of the road construction, and the taking of GPS measurements at certain points. It also includes his observations of the steep terrain and the presence of dry gullies, his observations of the absence of adequate sediment and erosion controls and, later, the failure of the batters and further erosion, and sediment travelling towards tributaries of Murdering Creek.
1. In these circumstances, the prosecutor contends that it was "abundantly clear" from the original summonses and the evidence provided with the original summonses that the essential nature of the prosecutor's case alleges "water pollution of dry gullies arising from the construction of roads" on Kiangatha's property. The prosecutor notes that the evidence "consistently" describes first, the road being constructed across dry gullies and on steep land where plumes of sediment occur downslope and towards dry gullies; second, the overall lack of adequate sediment and erosion controls; and third, a worsening of erosion over time. The prosecutor also notes that the allegation of "water pollution" was articulated in the three affidavits; the notice requiring information and/or records to be provided; and the notice of preventative action.
2. On the prosecutor's submission, the proposed amended summonses retain the essential nature of the prosecutor's case, because the prosecutor now alleges water pollution as a result of soil and sediment from a defined area of earthworks due to road construction polluting a single dry gully in each of the proposed amended summonses. The proposed amended summonses rely on the same underlying factual matrix set out in support of the original summonses. The change is that the prosecutor has amended and provided further particulars which go to the location within Kiangatha's property where the alleged offences occurred, which enable the defendants to more precisely locate the offences within the previous location of the constructed road.

Reduction of scope and election of a single allegation
1. The prosecutor submits that the amendments made in the proposed amended summonses effectively "restrict" the facts of each summons to a single allegation of water pollution. Notwithstanding the retention of the essential nature of the charge and the underlying factual matrix, the prosecutor contends that it could not elect a single allegation from the broader particulars of the road network and drainage lines of the original summonses without revisiting the essential factual particulars of the summonses.
2. In this respect, the prosecutor submits that the earlier particulars provided in relation to the original summonses are no longer relied on by the prosecutor, and new particulars have been provided. The prosecutor rejects the defendants' complaints regarding the differences between the particulars, characterising the particulars as "having changed by a matter of metres", and denying that this means the nature of the offences the defendants are being charged with has changed.
3. The prosecutor submits that the defendants cannot be prejudiced by the reduction in the scope of the factual matrix relied on in relation to the proposed amended summonses. This is because the prosecutor previously relied on the whole of the constructed road in the original summonses (in contrast to the specific parts of the constructed road now relied on) and the drainage network has remained the same.
4. The prosecutor refers the Court to a number of previous cases where the amendment of summonses following an earlier finding of duplicity has been permitted. In Snowy Monaro Regional Council v Tropic Asphalts Pty Ltd [2019] NSWLEC 182 Moore J considered the permissibility of amending summonses following a finding of duplicity to replace a reference to engaging in a course of conduct with a reference to a specific day. His Honour commented at [93]:
        "…amendment to allow for single-charge offences is permissible and should be made in the current circumstances. This is because the nature of the offence - being, carrying out development in contravention of a condition of development consent, in each instance - was known to the Company. …"
1. On appeal, the Court of Criminal Appeal commented in Snowy Monaro CCA (No 2) at [44]:
        "Faced with the decision of this Court [being the judgment of the Court of Criminal Appeal in Snowy Monaro Regional Council v Tropic Asphalts Pty Ltd [2018] NSWCCA 202 upholding Moore J's earlier finding of duplicity], Snowy Monaro has in my opinion permissibly sought to do no more than clarify the charges, by either nominating a single day upon which a breach of each condition is alleged to have been committed or by particularising every day upon which a breach of each condition is alleged to have been committed. I do not consider this to be an attempt to formulate a new or different charge: the offences alleged, being breaches of the relevant conditions of consent, stay the same."
1. The prosecutor seeks to distinguish the circumstances before me from two other cases where the amendment of the summonses was found to impermissibly enlarge the prosecutor's factual case. In Environment Protection Authority v Du Pont (Australia) Ltd (No 2) [2013] NSWLEC 99 ('Du Pont') at [30], Pepper J commented as follows:
        "…In my opinion the application to amend must be rejected for the following reasons:
        (a) first, in my view, the amendment will mean that the substance of the charge is not based on the same facts and the offence is therefore changed. Critically, the amendment will incorporate new campaigns of different products containing MSM than those understood by all parties to be the alleged source of the fugitive dust, some of which were processed in a different part of the factory, namely, at the DF plant. To date the focus of the preparation of the parties has been on dust allegedly emitted from the F&G plant during the April/May campaigns. By amplifying the charge period, the EPA will significantly enlarge the factual scope of the proceedings. In short, it will not be the same case;
        …"
1. In Secretary, Department of Planning and Environment v Goodman Property Services (Aust) Pty Ltd; Secretary, Department of Planning and Environment v Burton Contractors Pty Ltd T/as Burton Civil Engineering Contractors (No 2) [2021] NSWLEC 34 at [122], Moore J considered a complaint that "the now proposed geographic identifier (Catchment 1) was not an identifier arising out of anything pleaded by the Prosecutor with respect to the original defective charge against each of the Defendants". His Honour upheld the complaint, finding at [127] that the prosecutor's evidence in relation to the original charges did not include "material which would enable, by necessary implication, sufficient information that would permit the identification of Catchment 1 as a discrete geographic element of the site"; finding at [130] that the evidence would not permit the defendants to "discern the geographic location of the Prosecutor's now proposed to be pleaded offending conduct"; and further at [133], the now proposed mode of identification "only came into existence as an identifying concept able to be known to the Defendants … after the expiry of the relevant limitation period." His Honour concluded at [134]:
        "…the charge for which leave is now sought in the proposed Amended Summons does not constitute some appropriate and legally acceptable refinement of the earlier charge found to be defective but, correctly understood, constitutes a fresh charge laid out of time in circumstances where no sufficient information of a relevant identifying nature had been made available by the Prosecutor to the Defendants prior to the expiry of the statutory time limit."
1. The prosecutor submits that the circumstances before me constitute a permissible election of a single allegation in relation to each of the summonses, and this has involved a restriction of the previous facts relied on with respect to the original summonses. Such amendments would have "no doubt" been foreseen by the Court of Criminal Appeal in Kiangatha CCA (noting however, that the prosecutor rejects the defendants criticism that it inappropriately utilised the comments of Fagan J in Kiangatha CCA as a "prescription for the prosecutor to follow": Tcpt, 12 August 2021, p 78(14-16).

Amendment does not constitute a "fresh" charge
1. As explicated further at [106]-[114] below, the defendants contend first, the change in the locations of the alleged offences; and second, the inclusion of actual pollution in the likely pollution charges, means that the proposed amended summonses constitute fresh charges. The prosecutor rejects both these assertions, and submits that the proposed amended summonses do not constitute fresh charges.
2. The prosecutor's submissions in relation to the change in the location of the alleged offences have been summarised above at [81]-[82]. In short, the prosecutor relies on the scope of the evidence that was provided to the defendants with the original summonses, and the limited practical difference between the location of the alleged offences in the particulars provided for the original summonses and in the proposed amended summonses, to support its position that the change in the location of the alleged offences does not make the proposed amended summonses fresh charges. This submission also engages with the reference in Kypri at [24] to amendments being permissible where they clarify what is already apparent from the face of the charge (to the extent the prosecutor accepts that Kypri reflects the position in NSW).
3. In relation to the inclusion of actual pollution in the likely pollution charges, the prosecutor contends that this does not result in a new charge, because the placement of a pollutant that results in "actual" pollution of waters and the placement of a pollutant in the position where it might cause "actual" pollution are the same offence. The prosecutor cites Brownlie v State Pollution Control Commission (1992) 27 NSWLR 78 ('Brownlie') at 82, where Gleeson CJ commented:
        "There must be many cases in which a person places matter in a position such that it is likely to be washed into waters and then, subsequently, the matter is actually washed into those waters. That does not necessarily mean that the person will have committed two contraventions of s 16(1) [of the Clean Waters Act 1970 (NSW)]. Rather, it may mean simply that the prosecution will be able to rely on additional evidence. As a practical matter, proof that something is washed into waters will often assist a conclusion that it was originally placed in a position where it was likely to wash into those waters."
1. The prosecutor also refers to the analysis of Pearlman J in Environment Protection Authority v CSR Ltd (t/as CSR Woodpanels) [1999] NSWLEC 99; (1999) 103 LGERA 161 at [35], where her Honour considered the reference to harm and likely harm in s 6(1) of the Environmental Offences and Penalties Act 1979 (NSW) (repealed) and concluded that the section penalises a single act that may have a number of "forbidden characteristics", stating "[i]t is an act which is unlawful in specified circumstances, that is, where it harms the environment or is likely to harm the environment". By analogy, the prosecutor submits that it is the placement of a pollutant which constitutes the offence, whether it causes or is likely to cause "actual" pollution.
2. The prosecutor also submits that the inclusion of locations where alleged actual pollution occurred in the likely pollution charges is not new evidence, where the defendants have had the evidence of the three affidavits provided to them with the original summonses since October 2018, and this included evidence of actual pollution through the migration of sediment plumes from the road construction and the deposition of sediment and soil into dry gullies (including photographs).

Further issues of procedural fairness
1. Where the proposed amended summonses do not constitute fresh charges, but are nonetheless sought after the expiry of the statutory time limit for the alleged offences, the prosecutor contends that the focus becomes procedural fairness. This is because, provided no procedural unfairness would be suffered by the defendants, and the defendants are charged with offences known to law, amendments to summonses to cure defects such as duplicity are permissible: Built NSW at [47]; GPI (General) at [80]. It is uncontentious between the parties that the defendants have been charged with offences known to law, being water pollution pursuant to s 120(1) of the POEO Act: Tcpt, 11 August 2021, p 33(1-2).
2. Turning to the issue of notice to the defendants, the prosecutor refers to New South Wales (Department of Education and Training and Department of Juvenile Justice) v Cahill (No 2) [2011] NSWIRComm 33 at [125], and submits that the evidence in the three affidavits provided with the original summonses (which is also relied on in relation to the proposed amended summonses) makes it clear that the defendants cannot claim that they were denied procedural fairness in relation to preparing a defence to the proposed amended summonses.
3. The defendants raise changes to the landscape (as a result of further grading, installation of aggregate on the road surface, earthworks, or new or different sediment controls) in the time since the defendants were charged with the alleged offences as a procedural fairness issue. The prosecutor accepts that the landscape upon which the road was constructed may have changed by natural means or human intervention since the alleged offences were committed. However, the prosecutor notes that in circumstances where Kiangatha owns the relevant land and undertook the works subsequent to the alleged offences, the defendants would be able to understand the alleged offences and differentiate this from what occurred after the alleged offences.
4. Further, many of these issues would be present even if the summonses were not amended, in circumstances where the prosecutor previously referred to the whole of the constructed road (rather than certain parts of the constructed road) in the original summonses. The defendants have also not been prevented from conducting their own investigations of the construction of the road and its effects, with the prosecutor submitting that the fact that Mr Meyer was able to undertake detailed survey work in relation to the alleged offences on the defendants' instruction illustrates that the defendants were able to investigate the alleged offences.
5. The prosecutor also submits that despite the time since the original summonses were filed, the proceedings are still at an early stage as no plea has been entered and no orders for evidence have been made. The prosecutor notes that in Area Concrete Pumping, the Court held that an amendment did not cause procedural unfairness even after a plea had been entered.
6. In summary, the prosecutor contends both that the amendments in the proposed amended summonses can be made without injustice, but also that the amendments are necessary in the interests of justice. The prosecutor accepts that summonses should be framed with as much specificity as possible, to ensure the charges are clearly identified for the defendants: Cheung v The Queen (2001) 209 CLR 1; [2001] HCA 67 at [160]. In addition, if statutory provisions are subject to implied limitations, the prosecutor may be prevented from identifying a legitimate offence and possible offenders may escape penalty despite the chance of the possible offenders standing trial without unfairness.
7. Finally, the prosecutor rejects the defendants' criticism of the form of the proposed amended summonses. Instead, it notes that the proposed amended summonses include the aerial map which identifies the Sites, the composite aerial maps which identify the Sites and the location where ground-based photographs were taken, and then the ground-based photographs themselves.

Attendances and use of a drone to gather evidence
1. The prosecutor submits that attendances by authorised officers of Water NSW at Kiangatha's property and the use of a drone to take aerial photography to gather evidence during the proceedings are permissible in the exercise of Water NSW's statutory powers. The prosecutor rejects the defendants' contentions that the exercise of the statutory powers is affected by these proceedings or that gathering evidence constitutes an interference with the procedures of the courts.
2. The prosecutor refers the Court to Environment Protection Authority v Caltex Refining Co Pty Ltd (1993) 178 CLR 477; [1993] HCA 74 ('Caltex') at 558-559, where McHugh J commented:
        "Obtaining evidence under a statutory power for the purpose of assisting a party in pending litigation does not necessarily constitute an interference with the procedures of the courts. The evidence gathering procedures of a party are not limited to the use of court procedures. No interference with the processes of the courts or the course of justice occurs merely because a party avails itself of a statutory power to obtain evidence during the course of pending litigation. The mere use of such a power during the pendency of litigation is not a contempt of court even when the sole purpose of the exercise of the power is to assist a party to obtain evidence for use in that litigation. To constitute a contempt, the party must exercise the power in such a way that it interferes with the course of justice. Thus, there might be a contempt if the exercise of a statutory power "would give such a party advantages which the rules of procedure would otherwise deny him". But something more is required than that the party exercised the power for the purpose of obtaining evidence for use in pending litigation." [citations omitted]
1. The prosecutor also refers to Zhang v Woodgate and Lane Cove Council [2015] NSWLEC 10; (2015) 208 LGERA 1 ('Zhang') in support of its contention that the prosecutor's statutory powers should not be read down and limited following the commencement of court proceedings. As such, while accepting that the imposition of the stay by the Court of Criminal Appeal affects the actions that can be taken in these proceedings, it does not affect the exercise of the prosecutor's statutory powers.
2. As such, the prosecutor submits that the aerial photographs and survey information could be obtained by authorised officers of Water NSW pursuant to s 196 of the POEO Act, and no notice was required to be given to Kiangatha. The prosecutor draws a distinction between the circumstances in these proceedings, which do not adversely affect a right of the defendants, and the exercise of statutory powers to issue notices requiring defendants to attend interviews or provide information, which are contrary to the defendant's right to silence.
3. In this respect, the prosecutor criticises the defendants for their "bootstrapping" argument that because Kiangatha's common law property rights have been interfered with, ipso facto, there has been an interference with the course of justice: Tcpt, 12 August 2021, p 79(9-11). The prosecutor takes the position that the statutory powers specifically provide for the interference with common law property rights, and that property rights cannot be compared and elevated to a defendant's right to avoid self-incrimination (being the right that was infringed in previous cases). The prosecutor also contests the proposition that accessing Kiangatha's property gave the prosecutor a "forensic advantage", in circumstances where it was entitled to collect evidence using its statutory powers.
4. In any event, the prosecutor contends that the aerial photographs taken by the drone provide a "visual aid" only, and were obtained in order to accurately depict the location of the road, drainage lines, and ground-based photographs using GPS coordinates because the existing aerial imagery was inaccurate at higher resolution. This could have also been achieved by ground-truthing the existing aerial imagery instead of taking additional aerial photographs. In these circumstances, the prosecutor submits that it has obtained no advantage and caused no disadvantage to the defendants that would otherwise be prohibited by the rules of Court.

Defendants' submissions

Differences between the original summonses and the proposed amended summonses

Change in location of the offences
1. The defendants submit that the amendments sought in the proposed amended summonses "impermissibly" seek to materially change an essential element of the offences by changing the locations of the alleged action of pollution or likely pollution (where the new locations were not disclosed to the defendants before the expiry of the statutory limitation period, a procedural fairness issue discussed further below). The defendants point to Mr Meyer's survey work in relation to the geographic coordinates in the proposed amended summonses and his evidence in relation to the distances and topographic separation (as summarised at [65]-[66] above) in support of their contentions.
2. More specifically, the defendants contend that neither Site A nor Site B, being the alleged locations of acts of actual pollution which are identified graphically on composite aerial photographs and by geographic coordinates, were the subject of the original summonses as they are "physically removed" from the Red Dot Locations that were used to identify the location of the actual water pollution for the original summonses. Similarly, the defendants contend that Site C and Site D are "totally new" and are not coincident with the geographic coordinates provided for the closest Red Dot Locations in the original summonses. Finally, the yellow-shaded areas of the constructed road identified as the "approximate location of soil & sediment from earthworks" were not particularised in the original summonses.
3. The defendants reject the prosecutor's reliance on the "generic and wide-ranging evidence" of alleged water pollution in the three affidavits provided with the original summonses because this does not "disclose the essential nature of the water pollution alleged". Instead, they contend that:
         1. In relation to the actual pollution charges, the prosecutor particularised the location of the actual pollution charges with "a high degree of particularity and precision" in its response to the request for further and better particulars, and the defendants were entitled to proceed on the basis that these were locations of the actual pollution events (and not any other locations).
         2. In relation to the likely pollution charges, the "broad brush, inchoate and general terms" of the likely pollution charges did not inform a reasonable defendant of the true nature of the now very precise proposed amended charges that are sought to be laid.
         3. Responding to the submission that notwithstanding a degree of inaccuracy in the surveying the physical location of features remain the same, while this may be a philosophically correct position it ignores the need for a defendant to be informed of the location of water pollution, or the placement of sediment and associated likely water pollution, by a prosecutor so it can meet criminal charges.
1. The defendants note that the Sites are both a number of metres from the closest Red Dot Locations, and "physically quite distinct" from the closest Red Dot Locations by reference to characteristics of the locations. The defendants analyse the differences between each of the individual Sites and the closest Red Dot Location. For example, they contend that while Site A is located on an ephemeral creek line where the alleged constructed track crossed the creek line, Red Dot Location 2 was located 53.8m away and upslope.
2. The defendants submit that the differences in location, topography, and land features are not only relevant to the ability of the defendants to make out a defence of honest and reasonable mistake of fact, but also, in relation to the likely pollution charges, to the prospects of the defendants raising a reasonable doubt as to the proof of whether the pollution was likely to migrate from the point of placement to a particular stretch of the ephemeral stream. In this respect, the dynamics of water flow, sediment movement, and proximity of roads are crucial to any precise and scientific defence to the offences, but would change with any change in the locations of the offences. The defendants contend that the prosecutor did not provide sufficient notice of the new likely pollution charges prior to the expiry of the statutory limitation period (which they also raise as a procedural fairness issue, discussed further below). They ask the hypothetical question: "how on earth is the defendant expected to know that it is instead – will at some point in time be required to prepare a defence to an allegation of actual water pollution, the actual placement of material in a water course or ephemeral waterway these distances and across these topography changes?": Tcpt, 11 August 2021, p 38(17-21).
3. Finally, the defendants make specific submissions regarding the differences between the likely pollution charges in the original summonses and the proposed amended summonses. The defendants contend that the differences mean that both the locations where it is alleged sediment was placed from which it was likely to cause water pollution, and the locations where it is alleged that pollution was likely to occur (being newly identified Site C and Site D) have changed.
4. The defendants submit that in the original summonses the location where it is alleged the pollutant was placed was limited to the downslope edge of the constructed road (as the prosecutor's response to the request for further and better particulars on 4 December 2018 noted that the placement of sediment and earth was "on the lower side of the road"). In contrast, in the proposed amended summonses the approximate locations of the placement of soil and sediment from the earthworks has been identified by reference to newly identified yellow-shaded areas of the constructed road (bookended by specific geographic coordinates) which are not limited to the downslope edge of the constructed road. The defendants also contend that the location of the alleged actual pollution at Site C is upslope from the constructed road, such that the location where it is alleged that pollution was likely to occur apparently refers to the upslope side of the constructed road.

Reference to actual pollution in likely pollution charges
1. The defendants identify a further difference between the likely pollution charges in the original summonses and the likely pollution charges in the proposed amended summonses, being the inclusion of locations where it is alleged that actual pollution occurred. In this respect, the prosecutor's allegations in the original summonses involved the placement of material along the downslope edge of the constructed road which was likely to move into the waters (such that no allegation of actual movement of material into the waters was made). In contrast, the prosecutor's allegations in the proposed amended summonses are described by reference to newly identified yellow-shaded areas of the constructed road, and Site C and Site D are identified as the location of actual pollution occurring (where in the particularisation of the original summonses the closest Red Dot Locations 5 and 18 were locations of alleged actual pollution for the actual pollution charges, not the likely pollution charges).
2. The defendants submit that as a result of both the difference in locations and the inclusion of the actual pollution allegation the likely pollution charges in the proposed amended summonses are materially different to the likely pollution charges in the original summonses. They also contend that the inclusion of an allegation of actual pollution in the likely pollution charges is a "novel approach".

Amendments constitute "fresh" charges
1. The defendants submit that, taking into consideration the differences between the original summonses and the proposed amended summonses, the proposed amended summonses constitute an impermissible attempt to charge the defendants with fresh charges after the expiry of the statutory time limit for the alleged offences. This is because the proposed amended summonses materially change essential elements of the offences with respect to the locations of the pollution and also the inclusion of allegations of actual pollution in the likely pollution charges.
2. The defendants reject the prosecutor's reliance on the "factual matrix" when arguing that the proposed amended summonses are not fresh charges. They contend that it is the isolation of a particular location at which pollution occurred which is the "essential ingredient" of the alleged offence, and this could not be ascertained from the factual matrix. For example, Site C and Site D were "nowhere identified" in the original summonses and accompanying evidence, and photographs of the general area do not constitute "specification or identification" of the individual Sites.
3. The defendants also point to the prosecutor's express departure from the particulars of the alleged offences provided in December 2018 as an indication that the prosecutor is not electing amongst the multiple duplicitous offences already alleged, but rather creating a new charge. The defendants contend that nothing in the orders of the Court of Criminal Appeal in Kiangatha CCA would permit the prosecutor to allege a fresh charge, as this would be inconsistent with the underlying principle that fresh charges cannot be laid after the expiry of the statutory time limit. In this respect, the defendants criticise the prosecutor for adopting the comments of Fagan J in Kiangatha CCA at [68] as a "roadmap" for the process of electing a single offence and amending the summonses. Instead, they characterise Fagan J at [68] as discussing something that could have hypothetically occurred but did not occur, and now cannot occur: Tcpt, 11 August 2021, 35(49-50); 36(1-23).

Failure to give notice of the charges
1. The defendants raise the failure of the prosecutor to give the defendants notice of the charges (as amended). This is relevant both to the argument that the proposed amended summonses constitute fresh charges, (because they offend the principle that a defendant must be made to understand the "true nature" of the amended offence before the expiry of the statutory limitation period in Kypri), and in the alternative, the argument that even if the proposed amended summonses do not constitute fresh charges, it would be unfair and cause injustice for the proposed amendments to be granted.
2. The defendants contend that they were not given "proper notice" of Site A and Site B within the one year statutory limitation period for the offences, in circumstances where the defendants were first made aware that Site A and Site B (as opposed to Red Dot Locations 2 and 6) were the subject of the actual pollution charges when the notices of motion were filed on 7 May 2021: s 216 of the POEO Act.
